The energy per cubic centimetre on the average is

''The Pressure of Sound Waves.''—Sound waves, like light waves, exercise a small pressure against any surface upon which they impinge. The existence of this pressure has been demonstrated experimentally by W. Altberg (''Ann. der Physik'', 1903, 11, p. 405). A small circular disk at one end of a torsion arm formed part of a solid wall, but was free to move through a hole in the wall slightly larger than the disk. When intense sound waves impinged on the wall, the disk moved back through the hole, and by an amount showing a pressure of the order given by the following investigation:—

Suppose that a train of waves is incident normally on the surface S (fig. 11), and that they are absorbed there without reflection. Let ABCD be a column of air 1 sq. cm. cross-section. The pressure on <math>\text{CD}</math> is equal to the momentum which it receives per second. On the whole the air within <math>\text{ABCD}</math> neither gains nor loses momentum, so that on the whole it receives as much through <math>\text{AB}</math> as it gives up to <math>\text{CD}</math>. If <math>\text{P}</math> is the undisturbed pressure and <math>\text{P}+\varpi</math> the pressure at <math>\text{AB}</math>, the momentum entering through AB per second is <math>\int_0^1(\text{P}+\varpi+\rho u^2)dt</math>. But <math>\int_0^1\text{P}dt = \text{P}</math> is the normal pressure, and as we only wish to find the excess we may leave this out of account.

[[File:eb1911 v25 p0458 c1f1.png|center|175px]]
{{c|{{sc|Fig.}} 11.}}

The excess pressure on CD is therefore <math>\int_0^1(\varpi+\rho u^2)dt</math>. But the values of <math>\varpi+\rho u^2</math> which occur successively during the second at AB exist simultaneously at the beginning of the second over the distance U behind AB. Or if the conditions along this distance U could be maintained constant, and we could travel back along it uniformly in one second, we should meet all the conditions actually arriving at AB and at the same intervals. If then <math>d\xi</math> is an element of the path, putting <math>dt = d\xi/\text{U}</math>, we have the average excess of pressure
{{block center|<math>p = \int_0^1(\varpi+\rho u^2)dt = \frac{1}{\text{U}}\int_0^{\text{U}}(\varpi+\rho u^2)d\xi.</math>}}
Here <math>d\xi</math> is an actual length in the disturbance. We have <math>\varpi</math> and <math>u</math> expressed in terms of the original length <math>dx</math> and the displacement <math>dy</math> so that we must put <math>d\xi = dx+dy = (1+dy/dx)dx</math>, and
{{block center|<math>p = \frac{1}{\text{U}}\int_0^{\text{U}}(\varpi+\rho u^2)\left(1+\frac{dy}{dx}\right)dx.</math>}}
We have already found that if V changes to <math>\text{V}-v</math>
{{block center|<math>\varpi = \gamma\text{P}\left(\frac{v}{\text{V}}+\frac{\gamma+1}{2}\frac{v^2}{\text{V}^2}\right) = \rho_0\text{U}^2\left\{-\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{\gamma+1}{2}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2\right\}</math>}}
since <math>v/\text{V} = -dy/dx</math>.

We also have <math>\rho u^2 = \rho_0 u^2/(1+dy/dx)</math>. Substituting these values and neglecting powers of <math>dy/dx</math> above the second we get
{{block center|<math>p = \frac{1}{\text{U}}\int_0^{\text{U}}\rho_0\text{U}^2\left\{-\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{\gamma+1}{2}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2\right\}dx.</math>}} But <math>\int_0^{\text{U}}\frac{dy}{dx}dx=0</math> since the sum of the displacements <math>=0</math>. Then putting <math>(dy/dx)^2=(u/\text{U})^2</math>, we have
{{block center|<math>p=\frac{\gamma+1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{\text{U}}\int_0^{\text{U}}\rho_0u^2dx</math>}}
{{block center|<math>=\tfrac{1}{2}(\gamma+1)</math> average energy per cubic centimetre, (15)}}
a result first published by Lord Rayleigh (''Phil. Mag.'', 1905, 10, p. 364).

If the train of waves is reflected, the value of <math>p</math> at AB will be the sum of the values for the two trains, and will, on the average, be doubled. The pressure on CD will therefore be doubled. But the energy will also be doubled, so that (15) still gives the average excess of pressure.

{{c|''Experimental Determinations of the Velocity of Sound.''}}

An obvious method of determining the velocity of sound in air consists in starting some sound, say by firing a gun, and stationing an observer at some measured distance from the gun. The observer measures by a clock or chronometer the time elapsing between the receipt of the flash, which passes practically instantaneously, and the receipt of the report. The distance divided by the time gives the velocity of the sound. The velocity thus obtained will be affected by the wind. For instance, William Derham (''Phil. Trans.'', 1708) made a series of observations, noting the time taken by the report of a cannon fired on Blackheath to travel across the Thames to Upminster Church in Essex, 12½ m. away. He found that the time varied between 55½ seconds when the wind was blowing most strongly with the sound, to 63 seconds when it was most strongly against the sound. The value for still air he estimated at 1142 ft. per second. He made no correction for temperature or humidity. But when the wind is steady its effect may be eliminated by “reciprocal” observations, that is, by observations of the time of passage of sound in each direction over the measured distance.

{{smaller block|Let <math>\text{D}</math> be the distance, <math>\text{U}</math> the velocity of sound in still air, and <math>w</math> the velocity of the wind, supposed for simplicity to blow directly from one station to the other. Let <math>\text{T}_1</math> and <math>\text{T}_2</math> be the observed times of passage in the two directions. We have <math>\text{U}+w=\text{D}/\text{T}_1</math> and <math>\text{U}-w=\text{D}/\text{T}_2</math>. Adding and dividing by 2 <math>\text{U} = \frac{\text{D}}{2} \left(\frac{1}{\text{T}_1} + \frac{1}{\text{T}_2}\right).</math>}}

In 1822 a commission of the Bureau des Longitudes made a series of experiments between Montlhéry and Villejuif, 11 m. apart. Cannons were fired at the two stations at intervals of five minutes.
